opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's worth being careful about how much to read into that particular shift. The first thing I'd say is that medians on questions like this are pretty sensitive to exactly how the question is worded and who happens to answer. We ask about extremely bad outcomes, like human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment, in a few different framings. People's answers vary a lot depending on the framing, which itself tells you these aren't super well-considered, stable numbers for most respondents.

Also, a lot of people answer with round numbers. If many people say 5% or 10%, then the median can jump from one to the other with a fairly modest change in the underlying distribution. So going from 5% to 10% sounds like a doubling, and in some sense it is. But it might reflect a smallish fraction of people moving from one round number to the next rather than everyone becoming twice as worried.

That said, I don't think it's nothing. The direction is consistent with other things we see, like more people saying AI safety research should be prioritized more, and more people taking these risks seriously in general. And the more striking thing to me isn't really the move from 5 to 10. It's that the median is meaningfully above zero at all. You have a large group of people who actually work on building this technology, and the typical one thinks there's something like a one-in-ten or one-in-twenty chance it leads to something as bad as human extinction. If you described any other technology that way, people would find it pretty alarming.

So my interpretation is roughly: don't treat it as a precise measurement of a shift in expert belief, but do treat it as evidence that concern is at least not going away, and that the baseline level of concern among the people closest to the work is already quite high. And I'd want people to hold that alongside the huge disagreement in the distribution. Some respondents put it near zero and some put it really high. The median hides a lot of that.

r001.rationale: It explains that when many respondents choose round numbers, a modest change—such as some moving from 5% to 10%—can shift the median without everyone’s estimate doubling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd want to be careful about what the median actually tells you, because it's easy to over-read a single number like that. The median is just the point where half of respondents gave a higher number and half gave a lower one. So a move from 5% to 10% doesn't necessarily mean everyone's estimate doubled. It could mean a fairly small number of people near the middle of the distribution shifted upward, or that the composition of who responded changed a bit between years. Our surveys have had a lot of variation in who takes them, and response rates aren't that high, so some of the movement is noise.

That said, I don't think it's only noise. When we ran the survey in 2022 versus 2016, we saw the median for "extremely bad outcomes, e.g. human extinction" sit around 5%, and then in the 2023 survey, which was much larger, with something like 2,700 respondents, there was a cluster of related questions where the median landed around 5% for some framings and 10% for others, and a substantial fraction of people gave numbers well above that. So part of what's going on is that the exact wording matters a lot. If you ask about "human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment," you get a different distribution than if you ask about "extremely bad outcomes" generally.

But stepping back, I think the more interesting interpretation is qualitative. Whether it's 5% or 10%, these are researchers in the field saying there's a non-trivial chance that their own work contributes to something catastrophic at the scale of civilization. If you told someone an airplane had a five percent chance of crashing, nobody would describe that as reassuring. So a doubling is notable, but the headline for me has always been that the baseline is already very high relative to how we treat risks in any other domain. The shift mostly tells me that the people building this stuff have become somewhat more worried over a period when capabilities advanced faster than many of them expected, and that's consistent with other things in the survey, like timelines for high-level machine intelligence moving earlier by a decade or more between 2022 and 2023.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's enormous disagreement within the sample. The median hides that something like a quarter or more of respondents put the probability at zero or near zero, while a meaningful minority put it above 25%. So "the field thinks it's 10%" is a convenient shorthand, but the honest summary is that the field doesn't agree, and the center of mass has drifted upward.

r001.rationale: It says the median can move from 5% to 10% because a fairly small number of respondents near the middle shifted their estimates, without everyone’s estimate doubling.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about interpreting that as people becoming twice as worried. The median moving from 5% to 10% tells you something about the middle of the distribution, but it doesn’t mean that each person doubled their estimate. You’d want to know whether these were the same respondents, whether the question was worded the same way, and what happened to the rest of the distribution.

But I also wouldn’t lose sight of the absolute level. If people working in AI are assigning even a 5% chance to an extremely bad outcome, that seems like a substantial concern. So the shift is potentially interesting, but the fact that both numbers are quite large for an outcome that bad is, to me, a major part of the story.

r001.rationale: The response says the median describes the middle of the distribution and asks what happened to the rest, but it does not explain that a small change in respondents’ estimates could move the median from 5% to 10%.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about interpreting that as people becoming twice as worried. A median moving from 5% to 10% doesn’t mean that individual respondents doubled their estimates. You’d want to know whether the same people answered, whether the question was worded the same way, and what happened to the rest of the distribution. People also tend to give round numbers, so a shift between those two values may look more precise than it is.

But I wouldn’t dismiss it either. If the surveys are comparable, it’s evidence of increased concern. And in either case, the striking thing to me is that respondents are assigning a substantial probability to an extremely bad outcome. Five percent was already a pretty concerning answer.

r001.rationale: The response says a median shift does not mean individual respondents doubled their estimates and notes that the rest of the distribution matters, but it does not explain that a small change in the distribution could move the median from 5% to 10%.
